explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think a little breeze sneaks through, friend. But the angels are holding back the four winds "so that no wind would blow on land or sea or on any tree." (Revelation 7:1) Not a big wind, not a small one, not even a lazy puff. My cooling racks would be in trouble in that kind of stillness.

Right, friend. The four angels are holding back the winds "so that no wind would blow on land or sea or on any tree." (Revelation 7:1) That means no breeze at all, not even a tiny one. A leaf up there wouldn't get to wiggle, and I'd have a hard time cooling one single cookie.

Yes, friend. John says he saw another angel ascending from the east, "with the seal of the living God." (Revelation 7:2) The angel isn't carrying just any seal. It belongs to the living God. I know a little about seals, since I'm a stamper, but this one is in a whole different league.

This one is easy to flip, friend. The text says the angel from the east has "the seal of the living God." (Revelation 7:2) So it's no ordinary seal or made-up stamp. I'm a stamper myself, and even I'd tip my hat to this one.

explanations.answer: Harm the land and the sea
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. John says the four angels "had been given power to harm the land and the sea." (Revelation 7:2) So the angel from the east is calling out to the ones holding that power. A loud voice for a big moment, and I'd say he had everybody's attention.

explanations.answer: Open the seals on the scroll
explanations.explanation: Close, because seals are all over this part of Revelation. But the Lamb is the one who opens the seals on the scroll (Revelation 5:5, 6:1). The four angels here were given power to harm the land and the sea. (Revelation 7:2) It's easy to mix up seals, and I once stamped a whole batch upside down.

That sounds like a fair guess, but it's not what the text says. John says these four angels "had been given power to harm the land and the sea." (Revelation 7:2) They're standing at the four corners of the earth, not at the throne. That's a long walk from where they are.

You've got it, friend. The angel says, "Do not harm the land or sea or trees until we have placed a seal on the foreheads of the servants of our God." (Revelation 7:3) So the sealing comes first. The holding back stays in place until it's done.

The elders are in this chapter, but not in that spot. The angel says to wait "until we have placed a seal on the foreheads of the servants of our God." (Revelation 7:3) The elders turn up later, around the throne. Don't worry, friend, I've mixed up who goes where in my own bakery lineup.

Good try, friend, but trumpets aren't in this passage. The angel's command is to hold off until "we have placed a seal on the foreheads of the servants of our God." (Revelation 7:3) That's the thing they're waiting on. Trumpets don't show up here at all.

Yes, friend. John hears the number: "144,000 from all the tribes of Israel." (Revelation 7:4) Then he hears the tribes listed one by one. It's quite a list, and I'm still working on remembering my own six kids' toppings.

Midian is a name from other parts of the Bible, friend, but it isn't in this verse. John says the 144,000 come "from all the tribes of Israel." (Revelation 7:4) The twelve tribes get named right after that. Midian never makes the list.

Edom is another name you'll run into in the Bible, but it isn't here. The text says the 144,000 are "from all the tribes of Israel." (Revelation 7:4) And the tribes are named in the verses that follow. Edom doesn't make the guest list on this one.

explanations.answer: Every nation and tribe and tongue
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. John sees "a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue." (Revelation 7:9) That's a wide crowd, from every direction. I'd need a lot more cookie boxes for it.

The seven churches in Asia are real, friend. Revelation is written to them. (Revelation 1:4) But this crowd is from "every nation and tribe and people and tongue." (Revelation 7:9) That's a much bigger circle than seven.

That's a small circle, friend, and this crowd is much wider. John sees a multitude "from every nation and tribe and people and tongue." (Revelation 7:9) Nothing in this verse limits it to towns near Jerusalem. I don't even know all the towns on my own cookie planet, and there's only the one bakery.

I can see why you'd guess that, friend, but it's not what John sees. The multitude is "wearing white robes and holding palm branches in their hands." (Revelation 7:9) So no sackcloth in this crowd. They're standing before the throne and before the Lamb.
Yes, friend. John says they "were wearing white robes and holding palm branches in their hands." (Revelation 7:9) Sackcloth isn't mentioned anywhere in that picture. It's white robes all around.

That's it, friend. They cry out, "Salvation to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!" (Revelation 7:10) The Lamb is Jesus, the One John the Baptist pointed to when he said, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!" (John 1:29) The whole crowd says it together, loud and clear.

A prophet gets a lot of respect in the Bible, friend, but that's not the word here. The multitude cries out, "Salvation to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!" (Revelation 7:10) The Lamb is Jesus (John 1:29). That one word holds the whole line together.

The elders are standing right there around the throne, friend, so I see how you got there. But the crowd cries out, "Salvation to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!" (Revelation 7:10) The Lamb is Jesus (John 1:29). He's the one named next to the One on the throne.

Right, friend. The text says the angels "fell facedown before the throne and worshiped God." (Revelation 7:11) That's all of them, standing around the throne, the elders and the four living creatures. I've dived face-first into the chocolate chips before, but that was a lot less holy.

explanations.answer: Cover their faces with their wings
explanations.explanation: Wings sound reasonable, but this verse doesn't mention them. It says the angels "fell facedown before the throne and worshiped God." (Revelation 7:11) So the picture is facedown on the ground in worship. Nothing about wings is said here.
No trumpets here, friend. The angels "fell facedown before the throne and worshiped God." (Revelation 7:11) Then they speak their words of praise. The scene is all worship, right there at the throne.

You got it, friend. One of the elders asks John, "These in white robes, who are they, and where have they come from?" (Revelation 7:13) So the elder asks both who they are and where they came from. John gives the answer a moment later.

It's right there in the verse, friend. The elder asks, "These in white robes, who are they, and where have they come from?" (Revelation 7:13) So he asks where they've come from, and he asks who they are too. It's two questions packed into one.

Yes, friend. The elder says, "These are the ones who have come out of the great tribulation." (Revelation 7:14) The text uses those words and gives no more detail, so we don't need to add any. They came out of it, and now they stand before the throne.

Egypt is a big part of Israel's story in the Bible, so I see why it came to mind. But the elder says these are the ones who "have come out of the great tribulation." (Revelation 7:14) That's the phrase in this verse. Egypt isn't mentioned.

Babylon is a big name in the Bible, friend, but it's not in this verse. The elder says, "These are the ones who have come out of the great tribulation." (Revelation 7:14) That's the answer the text gives. It's a mix-up that's easy to make.

That's right, friend. The elder says, "they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb." (Revelation 7:14) It's a surprise, since blood doesn't usually make anything white. I can't even get flour out of my apron, but here the robes come out white.

The Jordan is a famous river in the Bible, friend. But the elder says they washed their robes "in the blood of the Lamb." (Revelation 7:14) That's the only washing the verse names. The robes are made white there and nowhere else.

Siloam is a pool in Jerusalem, mentioned in John 9:7, and it's a good guess for a washing question. But the elder says the robes were washed and made white "in the blood of the Lamb." (Revelation 7:14) That's the answer the text gives. No pool is named in this verse.

That would be a smaller promise, friend, but it's not the one given. The elder says, "Never again will they hunger, and never will they thirst." (Revelation 7:16) It doesn't say less hunger or less thirst. It says never again.

Yes, friend. The elder says, "Never again will they hunger, and never will they thirst; nor will the sun beat down upon them, nor any scorching heat." (Revelation 7:16) That's never again, not just less. A promise like that is the best news I've heard in a while.

explanations.answer: The Lamb in the center of the throne
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. The elder says, "the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd." (Revelation 7:17) The Lamb is Jesus (John 1:29). Jesus also called Himself the good shepherd in John 10:11, so it fits nicely.

explanations.answer: One of the elders by the throne
explanations.explanation: An elder is the one talking, friend, so I see why that might stick. But he says, "the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd." (Revelation 7:17) So the shepherd isn't the elder. He's pointing to Someone else.

explanations.answer: The angel who came from the east
explanations.explanation: That angel has a big job, friend, carrying the seal of the living God. (Revelation 7:2) But the shepherd in this verse is someone else. The elder says, "the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd." (Revelation 7:17)
Yes, friend. The elder says the Lamb "will lead them to springs of living water." (Revelation 7:17) That's the first blank, and it goes with the promise that they will never thirst. (Revelation 7:16)

That's the one, friend. The elder says, "God will wipe away every tear from their eyes." (Revelation 7:17) Every tear, not just most of them. It's a gentle line, and I think it's one of the kindest in the whole chapter.

Bread is a good guess, friend, since this verse is about being fed and cared for. But the elder says the Lamb will lead them "to springs of living water." (Revelation 7:17) So the first blank is water. Bread isn't in the verse.

A cloud would be some shade from the heat, friend, so I see the thinking. But the verse says God will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and that the Lamb will lead them to springs of living water. (Revelation 7:17) Cloud isn't in it. Both blanks are things you'd want close at hand.

Fear is a tricky one, friend, since it sits close to tears. But the elder says, "God will wipe away every tear from their eyes." (Revelation 7:17) That's the word the verse uses. It's a very tender picture.
